gip.definition: A hormone made in the upper gut after a meal. Like GLP-1, it tells the pancreas to release more insulin when blood sugar is high.

gip-receptor.definition: The receptor that the hormone GIP switches on. It is found on cells in the pancreas, in fat tissue and in parts of the brain.

dual-agonist.definition: One drug molecule that switches on two different receptors. Tirzepatide switches on both the GIP receptor and the GLP-1 receptor.

functional-antagonism.definition: When a drug that switches a receptor on is given for a long time, the cell may stop responding. The end result can then look like blocking the receptor, even though the drug is an activator.

receptor-desensitisation.definition: A cell's response to a signal gets weaker when the signal goes on and on. Often the cell pulls receptors off its surface or switches them off.

biased-agonism.definition: A receptor can pass on a signal along more than one route inside the cell. A biased drug switches on some of these routes more than others.

beta-arrestin.definition: A protein inside cells that binds to an activated receptor. It helps switch the receptor off and pull it into the cell.

receptor-internalisation.definition: When a cell pulls a receptor from its surface into the inside of the cell. Fewer receptors on the surface means a weaker response to the drug or hormone.

receptor-occupancy.definition: The share of receptors that a drug is bound to at a given moment. It is often estimated from drug levels in the blood rather than measured directly.

insulin-sensitivity.definition: How well the body's tissues respond to insulin. With low insulin sensitivity (insulin resistance), more insulin is needed to move the same amount of sugar out of the blood.

clamp-study.definition: A detailed test in which blood sugar is held at a fixed level with a drip. Researchers then measure how much insulin the body makes, or how much sugar it takes up.

adipocyte.definition: A cell that stores fat. Fat tissue is mostly made of these cells, and they also send hormone signals to the rest of the body.

c-terminal-amide.definition: The end of a peptide chain finished with an amide group (–NH2) instead of an acid group. Many natural peptide hormones end this way.

hypoglycaemia.definition: Blood sugar that is too low. It can cause shaking, sweating, confusion and drowsiness, and if severe it can lead to loss of consciousness.

prediabetes.definition: Blood sugar that is higher than normal but not yet high enough to count as type 2 diabetes. People with prediabetes have a higher chance of developing diabetes.

bmi.definition: Body mass index: your weight in kilograms divided by your height in metres squared. A BMI of 30 or more counts as obesity.

obstructive-sleep-apnoea.definition: A condition in which the throat keeps closing during sleep, so breathing stops or becomes very shallow many times a night. It is more common with obesity.

apnoea-hypopnoea-index.definition: The number of times per hour of sleep that breathing stops or becomes very shallow. It is used to measure how severe sleep apnoea is.

aliases: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
hfpef.definition: A type of heart failure in which the heart still pumps with normal force but is too stiff to fill properly. It causes breathlessness, tiredness and swollen ankles.

kccq.definition: A questionnaire that people with heart failure fill in about their symptoms and daily limits. Scores run from 0 to 100; higher means fewer problems.

hazard-ratio.definition: A number that compares how often an event happens over time in two groups. A hazard ratio of 0.80 means the event happened about 20% less often in the first group.

non-inferiority-trial.definition: A trial designed to show that a new treatment is not worse than an existing one by more than a set margin. It is not designed to show that the new treatment is better.

open-label.definition: A trial in which participants and doctors know which treatment each person gets. This can affect reported side effects and behaviour, such as eating less.

randomised-withdrawal-trial.definition: A trial in which everyone first takes the drug, and then some people are chosen at random to switch to placebo. It shows what happens when treatment stops.

maximum-tolerated-dose.definition: In a trial, the highest dose each person could take without side effects that made them stop. It differs from person to person.

dulaglutide.definition: A GLP-1 receptor agonist injected once a week, authorised for type 2 diabetes. It was the comparison medicine in the SURPASS-CVOT trial of tirzepatide.

narrow-therapeutic-index.definition: A medicine for which the amount that works is close to the amount that harms, such as warfarin or digoxin. Small changes in absorption can matter.

acute-kidney-injury.definition: A sudden drop in how well the kidneys work, over hours or days. Severe dehydration, for example from long-lasting vomiting or diarrhoea, is one cause.

falsified-medicine.definition: A product that pretends to be a real medicine, for example by copying its packaging or batch number. Its content, dose and sterility are unknown.

outsourcing-facility.definition: A type of US compounding facility registered with the FDA under section 503B of US law. It may only compound from raw drug substance if that substance is on an FDA list of clinical need or the medicine is officially in shortage.

gastroparesis.definition: A condition in which the stomach empties very slowly, without a blockage. It causes nausea, vomiting and feeling full quickly.

anaphylaxis.definition: A severe allergic reaction that affects the whole body within minutes. It can cause breathing problems and a sudden drop in blood pressure, and needs emergency care.

angioedema.definition: Swelling deep under the skin, often of the face, lips, tongue or throat. Swelling in the throat can block breathing.

inr.definition: A blood test that shows how long blood takes to clot. People who take warfarin or similar medicines have it checked regularly.

sglt2-inhibitor.definition: A diabetes tablet that makes the kidneys pass more sugar into the urine. Examples are dapagliflozin and empagliflozin.

metformin.definition: The most common first tablet for type 2 diabetes. It lowers the amount of sugar the liver releases into the blood.

insulin-glargine.definition: A long-acting insulin, usually injected once a day, that keeps a steady background level of insulin in the blood.

cohort-study.definition: A study that follows groups of people who already use different treatments, without assigning treatments at random. Other differences between the groups can distort the result.

gs-protein.definition: A switch protein just inside the cell. When a receptor is activated, the Gs protein turns on an enzyme that makes the messenger cAMP.

ileus.definition: A condition in which the bowel stops moving food and fluid along, so they build up. It causes a swollen belly, pain and vomiting.
